beats.narration: Begin by framing Foundations of AI System Architecture as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Consider this worked case: A learner maps the inputs, constraints, and observable result for Foundations of AI System Architecture, then checks each step against the stated claim. On screen, show a five-step pipeline diagram labeled Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, and Decision Rule. Annotate each node with a brief label and connect them with arrows to show sequential flow. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Foundations of AI System Architecture
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a five-step pipeline diagram labeled Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, and Decision Rule. Annotate each node with a brief label and connect them with arrows to show sequential flow.

beats.narration: Now define Image Representation in Computer Vision precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Consider this worked case: A 100x100 color image is stored as a 30000-element array where each triplet corresponds to red, green, and blue pixel values. On screen, display a small grid of pixels transforming into a matrix of numbers. Highlight one pixel and show its RGB values as a numeric triplet. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Image Representation in Computer Vision
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a small grid of pixels transforming into a matrix of numbers. Highlight one pixel and show its RGB values as a numeric triplet.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Color Conversion and Filtering operates in a concrete sequence. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Consider this worked case: Converting an RGB image to grayscale reduces three channels to one, simplifying edge detection. A Gaussian filter smooths noisy pixel values by averaging adjacent samples. On screen, show a side-by-side comparison: original noisy image, grayscale version, and filtered image. Use arrows to indicate the color conversion and filtering steps. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Color Conversion and Filtering
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison: original noisy image, grayscale version, and filtered image. Use arrows to indicate the color conversion and filtering steps.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Feature Detection and Calibration and make the decision criteria explicit. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Consider this worked case: SIFT features identify keypoints like corners and edges. Camera calibration maps real-world distances to pixel coordinates using known reference points. On screen, draw a grid of detected feature points on an image. Overlay a calibration grid showing how real-world distances map to image coordinates. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Feature Detection and Calibration
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a grid of detected feature points on an image. Overlay a calibration grid showing how real-world distances map to image coordinates.

beats.narration: Apply Geometric Transforms and Segmentation to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Consider this worked case: Perspective transform corrects a tilted photo. Foreground segmentation isolates moving objects from a static background. On screen, show a distorted image transforming into a straight, aligned image. Highlight segmented regions with different colors. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Geometric Transforms and Segmentation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a distorted image transforming into a straight, aligned image. Highlight segmented regions with different colors.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Motion Estimation and Object Recognition, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Consider this worked case: Optical flow tracks pixel movement between video frames. A face detector classifies detected regions as human faces based on learned patterns. On screen, display two consecutive video frames with arrows showing pixel movement. Annotate detected faces with bounding boxes and labels. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Motion Estimation and Object Recognition
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display two consecutive video frames with arrows showing pixel movement. Annotate detected faces with bounding boxes and labels.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Scene Understanding and Context with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. Consider this worked case: A kitchen scene is understood by recognizing a stove, a pot, and a person standing near the stove, establishing spatial and functional relationships. On screen, show a kitchen image with labeled objects and lines connecting them to indicate relationships (e.g., person near stove). Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Scene Understanding and Context
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a kitchen image with labeled objects and lines connecting them to indicate relationships (e.g., person near stove).

beats.narration: Use Evaluation and Robustness Testing to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Consider this worked case: An AI model is tested with images taken at different angles, under bright and dim light, with partial occlusions, and from different camera types. On screen, display a 2x2 grid of test images varying in viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Annotate each with the tested condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Evaluation and Robustness Testing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a 2x2 grid of test images varying in viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Annotate each with the tested condition.

beats.narration: Connect Practical Analysis Checklist to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Consider this worked case: A learner maps the inputs, constraints, and observable result for Practical Analysis Checklist, then checks each step against the stated claim. On screen, create a checklist graphic with six boxes. Check off each item as it relates to the pipeline components and evaluation criteria. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a checklist graphic with six boxes. Check off each item as it relates to the pipeline components and evaluation criteria.

beats.narration: Finish with CSCI-331: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence - Course Foundations Companion as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Consider this worked case: A learner maps the inputs, constraints, and observable result for CSCI-331: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence - Course Foundations Companion, then checks each step against the stated claim. On screen, show a five-step pipeline diagram labeled Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, and Decision Rule. Annotate each node with a brief label and connect them with arrows to show sequential flow. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

sources.excerpt: An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments are an integral part of the course. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

sources.author: OpenCV
sources.excerpt: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

sources.excerpt: Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.
